messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

As a park ranger, 32-year-old Kael had always been comfortable in the wilderness, relying on his wits and physical abilities to navigate the rugged terrain. But it was during a brutal interrogation while working abroad that his sense of self-reliance was shattered. Kael's captors had used torture to extract information from him, leaving him with deep-seated fears about his physical vulnerability. In the months following his release, Kael began to notice that he was rehearsing conversations before they happened, mentally preparing himself for every possible scenario in an attempt to regain a sense of control. He would script out what he wanted to say, anticipating potential questions and responses, but this strategy only seemed to heighten his anxiety. His feelings became increasingly numb, as if he had built a wall around himself to prevent any emotional pain from seeping in. Simple tasks like driving or being a passenger in a vehicle triggered a cascade of fears, and Kael found himself avoiding these situations altogether. He would take long detours on foot or bike, preferring the physical exhaustion to the perceived danger of being confined in a car. His colleagues at the park began to notice his changed behavior, but Kael couldn't bring himself to explain why he was no longer willing to participate in routine patrols. Delays of any kind – whether it was waiting for a bus or queuing up for coffee – sent Kael's mind racing with catastrophic scenarios. He would assume that something had gone terribly wrong, and his body would react before his rational thoughts could catch up. His heart would pound, his palms would sweat, and he would scan the surroundings frantically for potential threats. Even in the safety of his own home, Kael found himself repeatedly checking that doors and windows were locked, as if this ritual could somehow ward off the dangers lurking outside. When attempting to recount the events leading up to and during his torture, Kael struggled to articulate what had happened. Some moments stood out with excruciating clarity – the smell of sweat, the sound of screams in the distance – while others remained shrouded in a frustrating fog. He couldn't seem to put the experience into words, as if language itself was insufficient to convey the terror he had endured. Kael's faith in his own resilience had been shattered, and he now questioned whether he could ever rely on anyone else again. His reactions since the event – the hypervigilance, the avoidance behaviors – convinced him that he was losing his grip on reality. The thought sent a chill down his spine: he feared going crazy, succumbing to the very same darkness that had consumed his captors. As Kael navigated his daily routine, these fears and anxieties wove together into a tapestry of dread. He became withdrawn, avoiding social interactions and public spaces where he might be forced to confront his triggers. His work began to suffer as well; once an enthusiastic park ranger, Kael now felt like a shadow of his former self. It was the loss of his job – due in part to his increasing absences and inability to perform routine tasks – that finally prompted Kael to seek help. He knew he couldn't continue living in this state of suspended animation, constantly on edge and unable to shake the feeling of impending doom. With a mix of trepidation and hope, Kael walked into therapy, unsure what lay ahead but desperate for a way out of the darkness that had consumed him.
